body:
Not only does it not behave as with Godot Physics, but (as you can see in your MRP) you get met with an error in the Output pane saying:

```
Failed to build Jolt Physics box shape with {half_extents=(1.000000, 0.000000, 1.000000) margin=0.040000}. It returned the following error: 'Invalid convex radius'. This shape belongs to 'StaticBody3D:<StaticBody3D#2444876660670>' and 2 other object(s).
```

I could have sworn I had code to replace this `Invalid convex radius` Jolt error with one that mentioned collision margins instead, at least for the simpler primitive shapes, but as it turns out that particular code went away in godot-jolt/godot-jolt#406, when we added the dynamic scaling of the collision margin instead, which to some degree fills the same function, but doesn't cover the zero case. I guess I somehow never encountered a zero-sized box since then, nor ever had this error reported to me, because that will indeed trigger this error.

Either way, as it turns out, setting the cylinders to all have a zero height through a script (and thus a calculated collision margin of zero as well) does still seem to make Jolt behave the same as with Godot Physics, where the shape turns into a plane of sorts, which I'm surprised by.

When looking at the code for `JPH::CylinderShape` and `JPH::BoxShape` it would seem that there's a discrepancy within their error-checking, where `JPH::BoxShape` effectively checks for `min_half_extent <= collision_margin` (see [here](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/748edb70ed2f16b95af52f046781d57c242656a5/Jolt/Physics/Collision/Shape/BoxShape.cpp#L62)) whereas `JPH::CylinderShape` does `min_half_extent < collision_margin` (see [here](https://github.com/jrouwe/JoltPhysics/blob/748edb70ed2f16b95af52f046781d57c242656a5/Jolt/Physics/Collision/Shape/CylinderShape.cpp#L96-L106)). And indeed, changing the error-checking in `JPH::BoxShape` to also use `<` instead of `<=` resolves this problem and makes things behave as with Godot Physics (at least in this basic scene).

@jrouwe Is there some particular reason for this discrepancy in the error-checking? Are there other problems one can expect from a zero-sized shape like this, besides the obvious problem of having a convex radius of zero? I would imagine that dynamic bodies will be janky at best, but maybe it's fine-ish for static bodies, like in this MRP? Maybe we're better off just disallowing zero-sized shapes altogether?

@mihe No there's no particular reason for this. I've updated the code to change `<=` into `<`. 

I cannot recommend creating scenes like this though as these really thin objects make it easy for objects to tunnel through them.

> I've updated the code to change `<=` into `<`.

Great, thank you!

> I cannot recommend creating scenes like this though as these really thin objects make it easy for objects to tunnel through them.

Yeah, I figured. We should probably consider disallowing zero-sized shapes altogether, perhaps even on a physics server level, but for now just updating Jolt with this change seems like the path of least resistance to just resolve the discrepancy.

You'll find the update here: #101940

> Yeah, I figured. We should probably consider disallowing zero-sized shapes altogether, perhaps even on a physics server level, but for now just updating Jolt with this change seems like the path of least resistance to just resolve the discrepancy.

Can't CCD avoid tunneling issues when enabled regardless of the static body's thickness? It has a performance cost though, so it should only be used when actually needed.

My main concern is tunneling for discrete objects. CCD objects should indeed be fine and triangles indeed have the same risk of tunneling as a 0-volume box.

Most physics objects should not need CCD and it's much cheaper to turn it off. In that case, the thicker the box the better. The real world also doesn't have infinitely thin surfaces, so in most cases there should be room to make the box have thickness. It may be tempting for a content creator to create these thin boxes just because you can't 'see' the underside of the box (and we're all used to make levels with smoke and mirrors).

The only real worry with a 0-volume box is that `BoxShape::GetSupportingFace` will return a degenerate face when given a normal that touches the 'side' of the box. I'm hoping that all code paths deal with that properly (as far as I tested they do).
